judgments.reasoning_cat1: The obligation is defined entirely by reference to the Settlement Procedures plus 'such other action as is required of BD pursuant to the Settlement Procedures', so its content is external rather than ambiguous. No term here carries two meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its content depends wholly on the material incorporated by 2.1(b) (c010); if that incorporation is contested the duty is too, but no operative provision contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pass-through delivery obligation keyed to Section 2 of the Auction Agreement, with timing and manner also taken from that document. Definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It imports duties from the Auction Agreement while 3.1(b) (c030) confines the Auction Agent to duties expressly set forth or expressly incorporated 'pursuant to Section 2.1(b)' — which incorporates the Auction and Settlement Procedures, not the Auction Agreement generally. That is a small seam in the duty architecture.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: '.25 of 1% per annum as calculated below' plus 'may be adjusted from time to time with the approval of the Company upon a written request of the Broker-Dealer' leaves unclear whether adjustment requires agreement or merely Company approval of a unilateral request, and gives no standard or ceiling. The characterisation of the fee as 'compensation for the services of the Broker-Dealer in facilitating Auctions' is also capable of being read as conditioning the fee on services actually rendered.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That characterisation sits uneasily with 2.5(b) (c025), which entitles the Broker-Dealer to the fee even when 'an Auction was not held', i.e. when no auction was facilitated. That is a specific, nameable tension within the same section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The formula is long but mostly arithmetical; the notable defects are (B)/(5), which pay the fee when no Auction was held, and the closing proviso's reference to the definition of 'Broker-Dealer' 'contained in the Series 2004 Auction Bonds' — a misdescription of the source document. 'Conclusive absent manifest error' is also a term courts have to give content to.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 2.1(c) (c011) sources the Broker-Dealer definition to the Indenture, not to the Bonds, so the two provisions point to different instruments for the same defined term; and paying a facilitation fee for periods in which no Auction occurred is hard to square with 2.5(a)'s (c024) description of the fee as compensation for services. Both are concrete internal inconsistencies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence conferring an optional payment right on the Bond Insurer; 'right to pay' is plain and no condition is left open beyond non-payment by the Company. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits 5.5 (c036), which makes the Bond Insurer a third-party beneficiary, and 5.6(a) (c037), which requires its consent to amendments; the only gap is that it does not say whether payment by the Insurer subrogates it against the Company. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: BD must 'promptly deliver such funds to the party entitled to receive such funds' on a customer's failure — an unbounded backstop obligation with no cap, no time and no identification of the payee, and the closing 'no duty or liability with respect to enforcement' leaves the obligation unpoliced. 'Promptly' and 'the party entitled' are the nameable soft terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is keyed to the notice regime of 2.3(d) (c019), which the Auction Agent may refuse to accept if late, so a settlement departure could be left in limbo; and 2.6(b) (c028) disclaims responsibility of the Auction Agent, Trustee, Company and Issuer for the same failures. The pieces fit but leave BD carrying an open-ended risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A flat disclaimer naming four protected parties and the failures covered; 'or otherwise' is a mild catch-all at the end of the enumeration. Otherwise definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the mirror of 2.6(a) (c027), which puts those failures on BD, so the allocation is coherent across the section. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Auction Agent 'owes no duties, fiduciary or otherwise, to any other Person by reason of this Broker-Dealer Agreement' is stated absolutely, yet the same agreement imposes express duties on the Auction Agent to BD; read literally the disclaimer negates them. The sentence also ends without a full stop, and 'or in the Auction Agreement' appears to be a slip for 'or the Auction Agreement'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sections 2.2(a), 2.2(c) and 2.4(a)-(d) (c013, c015, c020, c023) all impose duties on the Auction Agent running to BD, who is 'any other Person' relative to the Trustee. Harmonising the absolute 'no duties' language with those express obligations requires reading in a qualification.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional express-duties-only clause with a precise cross-reference to Section 2.1(b); its terms are standard trust-indenture drafting. Nothing genuinely two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It limits incorporated duties to those coming in 'pursuant to Section 2.1(b)', while 2.4(d) (c023) imports delivery duties from Section 2 of the Auction Agreement, which 2.1(b) does not incorporate. That is a narrow but real seam.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Negligence or misconduct' is used without the usual 'wilful' qualifier and 'misconduct' is left undefined, and the two sentences state overlapping but not identical standards (no liability absent negligence or misconduct; no liability for good-faith errors of judgment unless negligent in ascertaining facts). Which standard governs a given omission is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to 'Section 3.2(d) hereof', a provision that does not appear in the instrument as it stands, and it sits alongside 3.1(a) and (b) (c029, c030), which disclaim duties altogether. The dangling cross-reference is the specific point.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Limb (ii) conditions legal action on 'indemnity satisfactory to the Auction Agent' and on what 'might, in its judgment, involve any expense or liability' — subjective standards that make the duty effectively optional. The enumerated (i)-(iii) list is otherwise specific.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with 2.2(b)'s (c014) disclosure carve-out keyed to indemnity satisfactory to the Auction Agent and with 3.1(b)'s express-duties-only rule. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A general standard ('circumstances beyond its reasonable control') followed by 'including without limitation' and a list of specifics that, as reproduced, breaks off mid-enumeration with a semicolon — the classic general-versus-specific problem plus an evident textual truncation. Whether unlisted events such as market disruption or auction failure qualify is exactly what ejusdem generis arguments are made of.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps the liability standard in 3.1(c) (c031), which turns on negligence, and a failure caused by circumstances 'beyond reasonable control' could still involve negligence; the two exculpations are not expressly reconciled. That is a modest overlap rather than a clash.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The notice machinery speaks of 'the other party' in what is a three-party agreement, deems telecopies effective on transmission rather than receipt, and requires communications to come from 'a BD Officer' and 'an Authorized Officer' — categories not defined in the visible text. The mismatch between 'party' singular and the tripartite structure is the nameable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The address block identifies the Issuer as 'HOSPITAL SERVICES CORPORATION', whereas recital c001 defines the Issuer as the New Mexico Hospital Equipment Loan Council — a direct inconsistency in the identity of a party whose consent 5.6(a) (c037) makes a condition of any amendment. That is a specific, checkable conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The integration clause extends to 'the other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds' — an unbounded set that is nowhere identified — and then denies any understanding 'oral, written or inferred', a formulation whose reach over implied terms is contestable. 'Inferred' in particular is unusual and open to argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be read with 2.1(b) (c010), which incorporates the Auction and Settlement Procedures in their entirety, and with 5.10 (c042), which negates implied duties only as against the Company; the boundaries of the 'entire agreement' therefore shift depending on which provision is applied. That is a real coherence question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause names the Auction Agent, the Bond Insurer and BD as the only Persons with any right, remedy or claim, and then preserves 'the rights expressly granted to the Issuer herein' although no rights appear to be expressly granted to the Issuer in the operative text; it also omits the Company, a signatory party. 'Nothing ... shall give to any Person, other than' is thus capable of being read either as an ordinary no-third-party-beneficiary clause or as stripping a contracting party of enforcement rights.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Company is a party to this agreement, is bound to pay the Broker-Dealer Fee under 2.5(b) (c025) and is given powers under 2.1(d) (c012) and 2.3(a) (c016), yet this clause denies it any 'benefit of any legal or equitable right, remedy or claim' under the agreement — that cannot be harmonised without qualification. The Issuer carve-out likewise refers to rights that appear nowhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A no-oral-modification clause requiring signature by each party plus written consent of the Issuer and the Bond Insurer; its requirements are specific and cumulative. Nothing ambiguous in the wording.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It requires the consent of the Issuer, a non-party whom 5.5 (c036) treats as having only such rights as are 'expressly granted ... herein' and whose identity 5.3 (c034) states inconsistently with the recitals. The consent condition is therefore harder to apply than it looks.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: By saying non-exercise is not a waiver 'with respect to any subsequent breach', the clause says nothing about the breach not acted on, and expressio unius invites the argument that the present breach is waived. That is a nameable general-versus-specific defect in an otherwise routine clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits with 5.6(a) (c037), which treats waiver as requiring a signed writing, so the two together largely close the gap; no genuine conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain severability clause with no reformation or essential-terms proviso; every term is standard. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No provision of the agreement conditions its operation on the validity of any other; no conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate counterparts clause, entirely definite. Nothing open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the signature block and with 5.6(a)'s signed-writing requirement; no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The United States District Court in the County of New York' names a court that does not exist by that title, and the sentence is ungrammatical — 'the parties agree that ... and that, in connection with any such action or proceeding, submit to the jurisdiction' has no subject — so whether the clause is mandatory or merely a consent to jurisdiction, and which court it designates, is genuinely arguable. Those are exactly the words two parties would read differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The forum clause binds 'the parties', which includes the Company, while 5.5 (c036) denies the Company any right or claim under the agreement, so the instrument is unclear about whether the Company sues here at all; nothing else in the agreement addresses venue. The tension is real though secondary to the drafting error.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause negates implied duties on the Company only, and does so across three instruments (this agreement, the Indenture and the Auction Agreement) to which the Company is not uniformly a party; 'duties, covenants or obligations ... not otherwise expressly set forth herein or therein' is clear enough in itself. Little internal ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Parallel disclaimers exist for the Auction Agent in 3.1(a)-(b) (c029, c030) but none for BD, which sharpens the argument that implied obligations of good faith attach to BD's undertakings in 2.3(b) (c017) and 2.1(d) (c012). That asymmetry is the whole-instrument point worth naming.
